title: Course setup
text: This course contains a few hands-on activities to aid understanding for some concepts we will cover. These have been designed to be carried out in R. To follow along, please make sure you have the following ready before coming to class.

title: Course setup
text:
1. Environment

Ensure you have the latest compatible versions of RStudio and R installed for your computer. If you have not previously used R/RStudio, you can install them using the Self-Service desktop application or by reaching out directly to JAX IT.
Make sure you have the following packages installed. Simply copy the code chunk and run it in the RStudio console:


install.packages(c(
  "tidyverse",
  "factoextra",
  "Rtsne",
  "uwot",
  "patchwork",
  "Seurat"
))

If Seurat doesn’t install correctly, you can install it through BioConductor as follows:

if (!requireNamespace("BiocManager", quietly = TRUE))
    install.packages("BiocManager")
BiocManager::install("Seurat")

That should do the trick!

To make sure the packages installed correctly, go ahead and try loading them in by running the following in the console:


library(tidyverse)
library(factoextra)
library(Rtsne)
library(uwot)
library(patchwork)
library(Seurat)

title: Course setup
text:
2. Data
We will be using the same dataset throughout the course. The original study sequenced 2,700 peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) from a healthy donor, which is freely available as the PBMC3k dataset from 10X Genomics.
A light-weight subset of this dataset is available as pbmc_small, which contains expression data for 200+ genes measured for 80 cells. utilizing a subset of the data helps ensure that all code can be easily and quickly run on most participants’ systems locally.
You do not need to download this dataset ahead of class, as it can be accessed after loading the Seurat package in our session.

title: Course setup
text:
3. Code
A Quarto document has been prepared and is available for participants to follow along with the workshop. It is recommended to download and work on this file. You will be using it throughout the workshop, and you can run through it line by line with the instructor and make any notes as needed.
To download it, click on this link to the participant notebook.
This will take you to the script on GitHub, you can download it by clicking the icon corresponding to ‘Download raw file’, as shown below:



Download icon for the script on GitHub


This is all that you need to get started!






Note



If you’d like to follow along with the class in real time, then please plan to come with these installed/downloaded. As this is a short workshop, we will not have time to troubleshoot software installations!

title: Linear Algebra for Biologists
text:
Course description
This is an interactive pilot workshop aimed at strengthening foundational linear algebra concepts in the context of biological data analysis. The focus will largely be on gaining an intuitive understanding of how biological data is structured and transformed in modern analysis workflows, including clustering and dimensionality reduction methods like PCA, t-SNE, and UMAP. Participants will learn how to critically evaluate their data, choose appropriate analytical methods, and derive biologically meaningful interpretations. This course is aimed at researchers seeking a conceptual understanding of the framework typically implemented in analyzing biological data. Open to all skill levels.


Prerequisites
Intro to R I and Intro to Biostatistics I preferred but not required.



Learning objectives
By the end of this workshop, participants will be able to:

Represent biological data as vectors and matrices
Interpret similarity and distance between samples
Understand how transformations affect data structure
Understand the need for dimensionality reduction
Explain the biological significance of computing eigenvectors and eigenvalues
Distinguish between popularly used dimensionality reduction techniques
Identify appropriate methods/techniques for specific use cases
Critically evaluate plots in practice




Course structure
The course has been divided into 5 modules and an optional take-home activity as follows:
Module 1: Understanding biological data structure
Biological data is often high-dimensional and can be represented using linear algebraic structures such as vectors and matrices. This module introduces how to think about biological datasets in terms of samples, features, and similarity.
Module 2: Data transformations
Preprocessing steps such as normalization, centering, and scaling can substantially change how data is represented and interpreted. This module explores how these transformations impact data structure and downstream analysis.
Module 3: Dimensionality reduction
High-dimensional datasets are difficult to visualize and interpret directly. This module introduces dimensionality reduction using Principal Component Analysis (PCA), focusing on intuitive interpretation and the biological meaning of principal components.
Module 4: Beyond PCA
While PCA captures global structure, it may not fully resolve complex patterns in high-dimensional data. This module introduces nonlinear dimensionality reduction methods such as UMAP and t-SNE, and discusses how they differ from PCA.
Module 5: Practical interpretation
This module focuses on interpreting real-world results. Participants will learn how to evaluate plots, identify potential artifacts (e.g., batch effects), and determine which analytical methods are appropriate for different datasets.
Optional: Exploratory analysis
Participants can apply the concepts learned in the workshop to analyze a new dataset, exploring its structure and drawing informed conclusions about underlying biological patterns.

title: Linear Algebra for Biologists Workshop
text:
How to use this notebook



This notebook is for you, the participant! Each demo is a self-contained code chunk, so all you have to do is run it. Feel free to take notes and add comments throughout the code, the idea is to have this document serve as a reference for you!

title: Linear Algebra for Biologists Workshop
text:
Setup
Run this chunk to set things up for the rest of the workshop. This should take less than 5 mins to finish running.

#load packages.
library(tidyverse)
library(factoextra)
library(Rtsne)
library(uwot)
library(patchwork)
library(Seurat)

#load dataset.
data("pbmc_small") #small single cell expression matrix, already log-normalized for our use.

#extract dataset we will work with, and convert to cells x genes format.
pbmc <- t(as.matrix(pbmc_small[["RNA"]]$data))

#extract metadata.
metadata <- pbmc_small@meta.data %>%
  as_tibble(rownames = "cell_id") %>%
  select(cell_id,
         cluster = RNA_snn_res.1,
         group = groups,
         n_counts = nCount_RNA,
         n_genes = nFeature_RNA) %>%
  mutate(cluster = paste0("Cluster ", cluster))

#checking:
cat("=== Ready ===\n")

=== Ready ===

cat("  Cells:", nrow(pbmc), "\n")

  Cells: 80 

cat("  Genes:", ncol(pbmc), "\n")

  Genes: 230 

cat("  Clusters:", paste(sort(unique(metadata$cluster)), collapse = ", "), "\n")

  Clusters: Cluster 0, Cluster 1, Cluster 2 

cat("  Groups:  ", paste(unique(metadata$group),   collapse = ", "), "\n")

  Groups:   g2, g1 








Expected output



Cells: 80   Genes: 230
If you see an error, make sure you have all packages, namely Seurat, tidyverse, factoextra, Rtsne, uwot, and patchwork correctly installed. Follow instructions given on the Setup page of the course website to do so if you haven’t yet.

title: Linear Algebra for Biologists Workshop
text:
Demo 2: Distance and dimensionality

#calculate distance matrix.
dist_pbmc <- as.matrix(dist(x = pbmc, method = "euclidean"))

#selecting cells in a cluster-specific way.
same_idx <- which(metadata$cluster == metadata$cluster[1])[1:2]
diff_idx <- which(metadata$cluster != metadata$cluster[1])[1]

cat("Same cluster: ", round(dist_pbmc[same_idx[1], same_idx[2]], 2), "\n")

Same cluster:  39.17 

cat("Different cluster: ", round(dist_pbmc[same_idx[1], diff_idx], 2), "\n\n")

Different cluster:  41.93 

#calculate average pairwise distance as dimensions increase.
set.seed(42)

dims <- c(2, 5, 10, 30, 100, 230)
data.frame(dimensions = dims,
           avg_distance = round(sapply(dims, function(n_dims) mean(dist(pbmc[1:10, 1:n_dims]))), 2)
)

  dimensions avg_distance
1          2         1.71
2          5         3.78
3         10         4.43
4         30         9.10
5        100        26.36
6        230        35.15








Discussion




What can you say about the cells that were used for calculating average distance with increasing dimensions?
What do you think will happen with multiple cell identities, and several thousands of measured genes?

title: Linear Algebra for Biologists Workshop
text:
Demo 3: Which genes are informative?

#calculating variance for each gene.
gene_vars <- sort(apply(pbmc, 2, var), decreasing = TRUE)

var_df <- tibble(rank = seq_along(gene_vars),
                 variance = gene_vars,
                 gene = names(gene_vars))

#plotting genes ranked by variance.
ggplot(var_df, aes(x = rank, y = variance)) +
  geom_line(color = "skyblue3", linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_point(data = slice_head(var_df, n = 8), color = "firebrick", size = 1.2) +
  geom_point(data = slice_tail(var_df, n = 5), color = "grey40", size = 1.2) +
  ggrepel::geom_text_repel(
    data  = slice_head(var_df, n = 8), aes(label = gene),
    color = "firebrick", size = 3.5, max.overlaps = 15) +
  ggrepel::geom_text_repel(
    data  = slice_tail(var_df, n = 5), aes(label = gene),
    color = "grey40", size = 3.5, max.overlaps = 15) +
  labs(title = "Gene variance across cells",
       x = "Gene rank",
       y = "Variance") +
  theme_classic(base_size = 12)














Discussion




What do you think the highly-varying genes tend to be? What about the genes that vary the least?
Should we use all genes for further analysis? Why, or why not?

title: Linear Algebra for Biologists Workshop
text:
Demo 4: Need for transforming data

#centering and scaling the dataset.
pbmc_centered <- scale(pbmc, center = TRUE, scale = FALSE)
pbmc_scaled <- scale(pbmc, center = TRUE, scale = TRUE)

#writing a plotting function.
make_scatter <- function(dataset, title, subtitle) {
  tibble(x = dataset[, "LYZ"], y = dataset[, "CD3E"], cluster = metadata$cluster) %>%
    
    ggplot(aes(x, y, color = cluster)) +
    geom_point(size = 3, alpha = 0.8) +
    scale_color_brewer(palette = "Set2") +
    labs(title = title,
         subtitle = subtitle,
         x = "LYZ",
         y = "CD3E",
         color = "Cluster") +
    theme_classic(base_size = 10) +
    theme(legend.position = "right")
}

#making the individual plots.
p1 <- make_scatter(pbmc, "Raw", "Original log-normalized")
p2 <- make_scatter(pbmc_centered, "Centered", "Subtract each gene's mean")
p3 <- make_scatter(pbmc_scaled, "Centered + Scaled", "Mean = 0, SD = 1 per gene")

#assembling figures.
(p1 | p2 | p3) + plot_layout(guides = "collect")














Discussion




What changed in going from raw to transformed data?
Did the relative position of points change?
What is another method you could use to judge the spread of your dataset before and after transforming it?

title: Linear Algebra for Biologists Workshop
text:
Demo 5: How many dimensions matter?

#run PCA.
pbmc_pca <- prcomp(pbmc, center = TRUE, scale. = TRUE)

#extract variance explained, and cumulative variance
var_exp <- pbmc_pca$sdev^2 / sum(pbmc_pca$sdev^2)
cum_var <- cumsum(var_exp)

#prepare dataframe containing information for scree plot.
scree_df <- tibble(pc = 1:40,
                   var_pct = var_exp[1:40] * 100,
                   cum_pct = cum_var[1:40] * 100)

#plotting.
p_scree <- ggplot(scree_df, aes(pc, var_pct)) +
  geom_col(fill = "skyblue3", width = 0.75) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:40) +
  labs(title = "Variance explained per PC",
       x = "Principal component", 
       y = "% variance explained") +
  theme_classic(base_size = 12)

p_cum <- ggplot(scree_df, aes(pc, cum_pct)) +
  geom_line(color = "skyblue3", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(color = "skyblue3", size = 2) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 80, color = "firebrick", linetype = "dashed") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:40) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 100)) +
  labs(title = "Cumulative variance explained",
       x = "Principal component", y = "Cumulative %") +
  theme_classic(base_size = 12)

p_scree / p_cum







#or, you can just run the following.
fviz_eig(pbmc_pca, barfill = "skyblue3", linecolor = "firebrick", addlabels = TRUE)














Discussion




What does % variance explained by each PC mean?
Where is the elbow for our data?
How much information is retained by the number of PCs chosen by examining the scree plot?

title: Linear Algebra for Biologists Workshop
text:
Demo 6: What drives each PC?

#extract first 2 PCs.
pbmc_pca_df <- tibble(PC1 = pbmc_pca$x[, 1],
                      PC2 = pbmc_pca$x[, 2],
                      cluster = metadata$cluster,
                      group = metadata$group,
                      counts = metadata$n_counts)

#plot PC1 and PC2.
ggplot(pbmc_pca_df, aes(x = PC1, y = PC2, color = cluster)) +
  geom_point(size = 3, alpha = 0.8) +
  scale_color_brewer(palette = "Set2") +
  labs(title = "PCA",
       x = sprintf("PC1  (%.1f%%)", var_exp[1]*100),
       y = sprintf("PC2  (%.1f%%)", var_exp[2]*100)) +
  theme_classic(base_size = 12)







#gene loadings for PC1.
as_tibble(pbmc_pca$rotation[, 1:2], rownames = "gene") %>%
  mutate(abs_PC1 = abs(PC1)) %>%
  arrange(desc(abs_PC1)) %>%
  slice_head(n = 15) %>%
  mutate(direction = if_else(PC1 > 0, "Positive", "Negative")) %>%
  
  ggplot(aes(x = reorder(gene, PC1), y = PC1, fill = direction)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.7) +
  coord_flip() +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Positive" = "firebrick", "Negative" = "skyblue3")) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "grey40", linewidth = 0.4) +
  labs(title = "Top 15 gene loadings for PC1",
       x = NULL, 
       y = "PC1 loading", 
       fill = NULL) +
  theme_classic(base_size = 12) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")














Discussion




Look at the top positive genes. What do you notice?
What are the top negative genes?
What is PC1 actually measuring biologically?

title: Linear Algebra for Biologists Workshop
section: Demo 7: Why preprocessing is needed for PCA
text:
Demo 7: Why preprocessing is needed for PCA

#PCA on non-transformed data.
pbmc_pca_raw <- prcomp(pbmc, center = FALSE, scale. = FALSE)

var_raw  <- pbmc_pca_raw$sdev^2 / sum(pbmc_pca_raw$sdev^2)

#scree plot.
fviz_eig(pbmc_pca_raw, ncp = 20, barfill = "skyblue3", linecolor = "firebrick", addlabels = TRUE) 







#PC1 vs PC2.
tibble(PC1 = pbmc_pca_raw$x[, 1], PC2 = pbmc_pca_raw$x[, 2],
       cluster = metadata$cluster) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = PC1, y = PC2, color = cluster)) +
  geom_point(size = 3, alpha = 0.8) +
  scale_color_brewer(palette = "Set2") +
  labs(title = "PCA: no preprocessing",
       x = sprintf("PC1 (%.1f%%)", var_raw[1]*100),
       y = sprintf("PC2 (%.1f%%)", var_raw[2]*100)) +
  theme_classic(base_size = 12) 














Discussion




Compare this scatter plot with the one we made before. What differences do you notice?
What are the possible reasons for this observation? How would you check?

title: Linear Algebra for Biologists Workshop
section: Demo 8: PCA vs UMAP vs t-SNE
text:
Demo 8: PCA vs UMAP vs t-SNE

#setting seed for reproducibility.
set.seed(42)

#extracting PCA scores to serve as inputs for the two methods.
pbmc_pca_scores <- pbmc_pca$x[, 1:10]

#running UMAP.
pbmc_umap_res <- umap(pbmc_pca_scores, 
                      n_neighbors = 15, 
                      min_dist = 0.3,
                      n_components = 2, 
                      verbose = FALSE)

#running t-SNE.
pbmc_tsne_res <- Rtsne(pbmc_pca_scores, 
                       dims = 2, 
                       perplexity = 10,
                       max_iter = 1000, 
                       pca = FALSE, 
                       verbose = FALSE)

#plotting outputs.
plot_embed <- function(x, y, title, xlab, ylab, show_legend = FALSE){
  tibble(x = x, y = y, cluster = metadata$cluster) %>%
    
    ggplot(aes(x = x, y = y, color = cluster)) +
    geom_point(size = 2.5, alpha = 0.8) +
    scale_color_brewer(palette = "Set2") +
    labs(title = title, 
         x = xlab, 
         y = ylab) +
    theme_classic(base_size = 12) +
    theme(legend.position = if (show_legend) "right" else "none")
}

p_pca  <- plot_embed(pbmc_pca$x[,1], pbmc_pca$x[,2], "PCA", "PC1", "PC2")
p_umap <- plot_embed(pbmc_umap_res[,1], pbmc_umap_res[,2], "UMAP", "UMAP1", "UMAP2")
p_tsne <- plot_embed(pbmc_tsne_res$Y[,1], pbmc_tsne_res$Y[,2], "t-SNE","tSNE1", "tSNE2", show_legend = TRUE)

(p_pca | p_umap | p_tsne) 














Discussion




Why do these three plots look so different despite working on the same set of cells?
UMAP and t-SNE seem to show more substructure within clusters. Does this indicate that there are potentially cell subtypes that were only revealed at this stage of analysis?
In which plot can you say something about how similar Cluster 1 and Cluster 2 are to each other? In which plots can you not?

title: Linear Algebra for Biologists Workshop
text:
Demo 9: Evaluating your embedding

#making a function to plot different attributes in the PCA plot.
plot_pca_factors <- function(color_var, title, colorscale){
  ggplot(pbmc_pca_df, aes(PC1, PC2, color = .data[[color_var]])) +
    geom_point(size = 3, alpha = 0.85) +
    colorscale +
    labs(title = title,
         x = sprintf("PC1 (%.1f%%)", var_exp[1]*100),
         y = sprintf("PC2 (%.1f%%)", var_exp[2]*100)) +
    theme_classic(base_size = 12) +
    theme(legend.position = "right")
}

#plotting the different comparisons.
p1 <- plot_pca_factors(color_var = "cluster", title = "Colored by cluster", colorscale = scale_color_brewer(palette = "Set2"))
p2 <- plot_pca_factors(color_var = "group", title = "Colored by sample group", colorscale = scale_color_manual(values = c("g1" = "skyblue3", "g2" = "firebrick")))
p3 <- plot_pca_factors(color_var = "counts", title = "Colored by library size", colorscale = scale_color_viridis_c(option = "magma"))

(p1 / p2 / p3) 














Discussion




Look at the group coloring — is there a batch effect in this data?
Look at the coloring by library size — Cluster 1 seems to have higher counts than Cluster 0. Does that mean the normalization failed, or could this be biological?
What would be more worrying to you — if group perfectly separated the clusters, or if library size did?

title: Linear Algebra for Biologists Workshop
text:
Demo 10: Parameters matter

run_umap <- function(nn){
  set.seed(42)
  umap(pbmc_pca_scores, 
       n_neighbors = nn, 
       min_dist = 0.3,
       n_components = 2, 
       verbose = FALSE)
}

p1 <- plot_embed(run_umap(5)[,1], run_umap(5)[,2], "n_neighbors = 5", "UMAP1", "UMAP2")
p2 <- plot_embed(run_umap(15)[,1], run_umap(15)[,2], "n_neighbors = 15", "UMAP1", "UMAP2")
p3 <- plot_embed(run_umap(30)[,1], run_umap(30)[,2], "n_neighbors = 30", "UMAP1", "UMAP2", show_legend = TRUE)

(p1 | p2 | p3)














Discussion




The clusters look most dramatically separated in n_neighbors = 5. Does that mean it’s the best parameter choice?
In n_neighbors = 30, Clusters 0 and 2 have merged into a diagonal. What does that tell you about what happens when neighborhoods get too large?
If you saw only the n_neighbors = 5 plot in a paper, what would you conclude about the number of cell populations? Would that conclusion hold across all three plots?
